teaser: The best seat at Niagara Falls is one where no human could ever stand.
review_notes:
This catalog image is a gallery photograph that includes the gold frame at the edges and has some glare; colors are duller than the painting.
Size about 101.6 x 229.9 cm.
Ruskin anecdote about the rainbow (he reportedly looked for light coming through a window) is traditional; check.
Exhibited New York 1857 at Williams, Stevens & Williams, 25-cent admission; then London; awarded a medal at the 1867 Paris Exposition Universelle.
Bought by William Wilson Corcoran in 1876 for $12,500; transferred to the NGA after the Corcoran Gallery closed in 2014.
Terrapin Tower: the tiny pale vertical near the left end of the falls (about x 0.125, y 0.42) is very small in this image.

lesson.text: Something in this picture does not add up. It is painted with the care of a survey: every ripple, every shade of green, the far shore ruled across like a pencil line. Yet the place it puts you does not exist. There is no rock under your feet, no railing, no bank. You are hanging in the air a few steps from the brink.

Earlier painters of Niagara had always given viewers somewhere safe to stand: a ledge, a clump of trees, a few tourists pointing. Frederic Church, in 1857, cut all of that away. The bottom edge of his canvas is water, already sliding toward the drop.

He also chose a strange shape. The canvas is about 1 meter high and 2.3 meters long (3.5 by 7.5 feet), more than twice as wide as it is tall. A painting that wide cannot be taken in at once, so your head has to turn, as it would at the real falls.
Three lines explain how Church built so much space from so few elements.

lines.label: The horizon
lines.text: A dead-straight far shore, set above the middle of the canvas. More than half the picture is therefore water, and the level line makes the curve below it feel even more unstable.

lines.label: The horseshoe
lines.text: The rim of the falls runs across and then hooks back toward you on the right. That bend is why the Canadian fall is called the Horseshoe. Church shows it from the Canadian side.

lines.label: The near edge
lines.text: Here the river, dark green and rising like a hill, tips over into white vapor. Follow this line with your eye and you will feel the drop that the painting never actually shows.

lesson.text: We never see the bottom. The plunge is hidden in mist, and Church lets the sound and the depth happen in your imagination. What he does paint, with enormous patience, is the surface: glassy where the water is deep, torn white where it hits rock.
Church visited the falls several times in 1856, sketching from both banks in pencil and oil. The big canvas itself then went fast: he is said to have finished it in under two months.
He was 31, and already known for accuracy. But a wide strip of rushing water could easily have been monotonous. So he planted a few small events in it, each one doing a specific job.

lesson.title: Small things, big jobs
lesson.text: Three details keep this ocean of water from going flat.

spots.title: The rainbow
spots.text: An arc of color stands in the spray, broken off partway. Its other end reappears high in the dark sky at the upper left. A rainbow needs sun behind you, so it tells you where the light is.

spots.title: The drifting tree
spots.text: A bare trunk with its roots in the air is caught in the rapids at the very bottom. It is the only solid object near you, and seconds from going over. It gives the scale, and the dread.

spots.title: A speck of tower
spots.text: At the far left end of the rim, a tiny pale upright marks a stone lookout tower that tourists climbed in the 1850s. It is the single trace of the crowds Church left out.

lesson.text: That tower matters more than its size. By 1857 Niagara was the busiest tourist site in North America, ringed with hotels, stairs and souvenir stands. Church showed the falls as if they had only just been discovered and reduced the tourist trade to one speck on the horizon.

When the painting traveled to London, the critic John Ruskin, a famously hard man to impress, is said to have checked the gallery window. He suspected the rainbow was real light falling on the canvas.

In New York the picture was shown alone in a commercial gallery, and tens of thousands of people paid to file past it. Color prints of it sold widely. For many Americans who would never afford the trip, this canvas was Niagara.
Church took away the ground under the viewer. With no foreground to stand on, you stop being a spectator of the falls and feel like something the river is carrying.

The falls were also a national emblem, the one natural wonder the young United States could set against Europe's cathedrals and ruins. Sent to the 1867 world's fair in Paris, the painting won a medal, and European critics conceded that American art had arrived.

In 1876 a Washington banker, William Corcoran, bought the canvas at auction for $12,500, a record sum for an American painting at the time. It stayed in his gallery until that museum closed in 2014, then moved across town to the National Gallery.

Go back to the driftwood at the bottom edge. Church painted it in the last moment before it disappears. It has now stayed there for more than a century and a half, and you are still in the air above it.

quiz.question: What did Church remove that earlier views of Niagara always had?
options: A safe foreground for the viewer to stand on
quiz.explanation: He cut away any ledge or bank, leaving the viewer over the water.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the canvas's shape?
options: It is more than twice as wide as it is tall
It is taller than it is wide
quiz.explanation: About 1 by 2.3 meters, it forces your eyes to sweep sideways.

quiz.question: What solid object is caught in the rapids at the bottom?
quiz.explanation: An uprooted trunk drifts toward the edge and gives a sense of scale.

quiz.question: Which part of the falls does the painting never show?
quiz.explanation: The plunge disappears into mist and is left to imagination.

quiz.question: What did the critic John Ruskin reportedly suspect in London?
options: That the rainbow was real light from a window
That the painting was a photograph
That Church had never been to Niagara
quiz.explanation: He is said to have checked whether light was falling on the canvas.

facts.text: Church filled the foreground with tourists to show how popular the falls were.
facts.explanation: He left people out entirely; only a tiny distant tower hints at tourism.

facts.text: The painting won a medal at the 1867 world's fair in Paris.
facts.explanation: It was sent to the Paris exposition and was honored there.

facts.text: The horizon in the painting is a straight line set above the middle of the canvas.
facts.explanation: The level far shore leaves more than half the picture to water.
